putnam-2004-a1.title: Look at the crossing step
putnam-2004-a1.body:
**Yes.** Suppose not: $S(N) \ne \frac45N$ for all $N$ in between. Let $N_1 < N_2$ with $S(N_1) < \frac45N_1$ and $S(N_2) > \frac45 N_2$, and let $N$ be the largest integer in $[N_1, N_2)$ with $S(N) < \frac45N$. Then $S(N+1) \ge \frac45(N+1)$, hence $S(N+1) > \frac45(N+1)$ by assumption.

Let $m = S(N)$. Since $S(N+1) \le m + 1$:
$$5m < 4N \qquad\text{and}\qquad 5(m+1) \ge 5S(N+1) > 4(N+1),\ \text{ i.e. } 4N < 5m+1 .$$
So the integer $4N$ lies strictly between the consecutive integers $5m$ and $5m+1$, which is impossible. Hence at some moment $S(N) = \frac45N$ exactly. ∎

*Remark.* The same argument works for any fraction $\frac{n-1}{n}$, but not for other fractions. For example, with $60\%$: missing the first throw and making the next two gives $0\%$, $50\%$, $66.7\%$, jumping over $60\%$.

putnam-2004-a2.title: Compare one pair of angles
putnam-2004-a2.body:
**Yes.** Let $\alpha_i, \beta_i, \gamma_i$ be the angles of $T_i$ opposite the sides $a_i, b_i, c_i$. Since $\alpha_1+\beta_1+\gamma_1 = \pi = \alpha_2+\beta_2+\gamma_2$, at least one angle of $T_1$ is $\le$ the corresponding angle of $T_2$; by symmetry of the roles, say $\alpha_1 \le \alpha_2$.

Because $T_2$ is acute, $0 < \alpha_1 \le \alpha_2 < \frac\pi2$, and $\sin$ is increasing on $[0,\frac\pi2]$, so $\sin\alpha_1 \le \sin\alpha_2$. The angle $\alpha_i$ lies between the sides $b_i$ and $c_i$, so
$$A_1 = \tfrac12 b_1c_1\sin\alpha_1 \le \tfrac12 b_2c_2\sin\alpha_2 = A_2 . \qquad ∎$$

*Remark.* The acuteness hypothesis is needed: $T_2$ with sides $1, 1, 1.9$ has area about $0.30$, while $T_1$ with sides $1, 1, \sqrt2$ has area $0.5$.

putnam-2004-a2.title: Fix a common side first
putnam-2004-a2.body:
**Yes.** Let $P_i, Q_i, R_i$ be the vertices of $T_i$ opposite $a_i, b_i, c_i$.

**Special case $a_1 = a_2$.** Place both triangles with $Q_1 = Q_2$, $R_1 = R_2$ on the $x$-axis and $P_1, P_2$ above it. Since the angles of $T_2$ at $Q_2$ and $R_2$ are acute, the foot of the altitude from $P_2$ lies strictly between them; choose coordinates with that foot at the origin:
$$Q_2 = (-q,0),\quad R_2 = (r,0),\quad P_2 = (0,H),\qquad q,r,H>0,$$
and let $P_1 = (s,t)$, $t>0$. Recall $P_iQ_i = c_i$ and $P_iR_i = b_i$. Suppose $t > H$.
- If $s\ge0$: $P_1Q_2^2 = (s+q)^2 + t^2 > q^2 + H^2 = c_2^2$, contradicting $c_1\le c_2$.
- If $s<0$: $P_1R_2^2 = (r-s)^2 + t^2 > r^2 + H^2 = b_2^2$, contradicting $b_1\le b_2$.

So $t\le H$, and $A_1 = \frac12 a_1t \le \frac12 a_2H = A_2$.

**General case.** Let $r = \max\{a_1/a_2, b_1/b_2, c_1/c_2\} \le 1$, say $r = a_1/a_2$. The triangle $T_3$ with sides $ra_2, rb_2, rc_2$ is similar to $T_2$ (hence acute) with area $r^2A_2$, and $T_1$, $T_3$ satisfy the special case ($a_1 = ra_2$, $b_1 \le rb_2$, $c_1\le rc_2$). So $A_1 \le r^2 A_2 \le A_2$. ∎

putnam-2004-a3.title: Guess a double factorial and verify
putnam-2004-a3.body:
The condition reads $u_nu_{n+3} - u_{n+1}u_{n+2} = n!$, so as long as $u_n \ne 0$,
$$u_{n+3} = \frac{n! + u_{n+1}u_{n+2}}{u_n}.$$
Computing: $u_3 = 2$, $u_4 = 3$, $u_5 = 8$, $u_6 = 15$, $u_7 = 48$, … which suggests double factorials. For $m \ge 0$ let $m!! = m(m-2)(m-4)\cdots$ (ending at $2$ or $1$, with $0!! = 1$), and put $w_n = (n-1)!!$ for $n\ge1$. Note
$$(n-1)!!\cdot n!! = n!,\qquad (n+1)!! = (n+1)(n-1)!!,\qquad (n+2)!! = (n+2)\,n!! .$$
Hence for $n\ge1$:
$$w_nw_{n+3} = (n-1)!!\,(n+2)!! = (n+2)\,(n-1)!!\,n!! = (n+2)\,n!,$$
$$w_{n+1}w_{n+2} = n!!\,(n+1)!! = (n+1)\,n!!\,(n-1)!! = (n+1)\,n!,$$
so $w_nw_{n+3} - w_{n+1}w_{n+2} = n!$.

**Induction.** $u_1 = 1 = w_1$, $u_2 = 1 = w_2$, and from $n = 0$: $u_3 = (0! + u_1u_2)/u_0 = 2 = w_3$. If $u_k = w_k$ for $k = n, n+1, n+2$ (some $n\ge1$), then since $w_n > 0$,
$$u_{n+3} = \frac{n! + w_{n+1}w_{n+2}}{w_n} = w_{n+3}.$$
So $u_n = w_n$ for all $n\ge1$ (and $u_0 = 1$); in particular every $u_n$ is a positive integer (and all the divisions in the recursion are legitimate). ∎

putnam-2004-a4.title: Average over all sign patterns
putnam-2004-a4.body:
We prove the identity
$$x_1\cdots x_n = \frac{1}{2^n\,n!}\sum_{e\in\{-1,1\}^n} e_1e_2\cdots e_n\,(e_1x_1 + \cdots + e_nx_n)^n ,$$
which has the required form with $N = 2^n$, $a_{ij} = e_j$ and $c = \pm\frac{1}{2^nn!}$.

By the multinomial theorem, $(e_1x_1+\cdots+e_nx_n)^n = \sum_{|\alpha| = n}\frac{n!}{\alpha!}e^\alpha x^\alpha$, where $\alpha = (\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n)$ has nonnegative entries summing to $n$, $e^\alpha = \prod e_j^{\alpha_j}$, $\alpha! = \prod\alpha_j!$. So the coefficient of $x^\alpha$ on the right side is $\frac{1}{2^n\alpha!}\sum_e e_1\cdots e_n e^\alpha$, and
$$\sum_{e\in\{\pm1\}^n}\prod_{j=1}^n e_j^{\alpha_j+1} = \prod_{j=1}^n\left(1 + (-1)^{\alpha_j+1}\right) = \begin{cases}2^n & \text{all }\alpha_j \text{ odd},\\ 0 & \text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$$
If all $\alpha_j$ are odd then all are $\ge1$, and $\sum\alpha_j = n$ forces $\alpha = (1,\dots,1)$, with $\alpha! = 1$. Hence the right side equals $\frac{2^n}{2^n}x_1\cdots x_n = x_1\cdots x_n$. ∎

putnam-2004-a4.title: Inclusion–exclusion over subsets
putnam-2004-a4.body:
Another valid identity uses coefficients $0,1$ only:
$$x_1\cdots x_n = \frac{1}{n!}\sum_{S\subseteq\{1,\dots,n\}}(-1)^{n-|S|}\Big(\sum_{j\in S}x_j\Big)^n \qquad (N = 2^n).$$
Expand $\left(\sum_{j\in S}x_j\right)^n = \sum_{|\alpha| = n,\ \mathrm{supp}\,\alpha\subseteq S}\frac{n!}{\alpha!}x^\alpha$. For a fixed $\alpha$ with support $T$, the coefficient of $x^\alpha$ on the right is
$$\frac{1}{\alpha!}\sum_{S\supseteq T}(-1)^{n-|S|} = \frac{1}{\alpha!}(1-1)^{n-|T|},$$
which is $0$ unless $T = \{1,\dots,n\}$. With full support and $|\alpha| = n$ we must have $\alpha = (1,\dots,1)$, coefficient $1$. ∎

putnam-2004-a5.title: Components ≥ vertices − edges, corrected by 2×2 blocks
putnam-2004-a5.body:
**A graph lemma.** A graph with $V$ vertices and $E$ edges has at least $V - E$ connected components: start with no edges ($V$ components) and add edges one at a time; each edge reduces the number of components by at most $1$. Moreover, removing an edge that lies on a cycle does not change the components.

**The graph.** Let $G$ have the $mn$ squares as vertices, two squares joined when they share a side and have the same colour. The monochromatic regions are exactly the components of $G$. Let $A$ be the number of edges of $G$ and $B$ the number of monochromatic $2\times2$ blocks. Each such block gives a $4$-cycle in $G$. Process the monochromatic blocks from the bottom row of blocks to the top, and for each delete its **bottom** edge (joining its two lower squares). Different blocks have different bottom edges. When the block whose top squares lie in row $i$ is processed, only horizontal edges in rows $\ge i+1$ have been deleted, so the other three edges of its $4$-cycle (two vertical ones and the top one, in row $i$) are still present; hence each deletion removes an edge on a cycle and keeps the components unchanged. The final graph has $mn$ vertices and $A - B$ edges, so
$$\#\text{regions} \ \ge\ mn - A + B .$$

**Expectations.** There are $m(n-1) + (m-1)n$ pairs of adjacent squares, each monochromatic with probability $\frac12$, and $(m-1)(n-1)$ blocks of $2\times2$, each monochromatic with probability $\frac{2}{16} = \frac18$. By linearity of expectation,
$$\mathbb E[\#\text{regions}] \ge mn - \tfrac12\left(2mn - m - n\right) + \tfrac18(m-1)(n-1) = \frac{mn + 3m + 3n + 1}{8} > \frac{mn}{8}. \qquad ∎$$

putnam-2004-a5.title: Add the squares one at a time
putnam-2004-a5.body:
Number the squares row by row (left to right, top row first) and let $X_i$ be the number of monochromatic regions of the figure formed by the first $i$ squares. We show $\mathbb E[X_i - X_{i-1}] \ge \frac18$ for each $i$ (with $X_0 = 0$), which gives $\mathbb E[X_{mn}] \ge \frac{mn}{8}$, and the first step gives strictly more.

When square $i$ is added, it is adjacent (among earlier squares) only to the square above it and/or the square to its left.
- **First square:** $X_1 - X_0 = 1$.
- **Only one earlier neighbour** (top row or left column): a new region is created if the colours differ (probability $\frac12$), otherwise nothing changes. Expected change $\frac12$.
- **Two earlier neighbours** (above $U$ and left $L$; let $D$ be the square diagonally up-left). If square $i$ differs from both $U$ and $L$ (probability $\frac14$), it forms a new region: $+1$. If it agrees with exactly one of them, it just joins that region: $0$. If it agrees with both, it can merge two regions into one ($-1$) or join a single region ($0$); merging is impossible if $D$ also has this colour, since then $U, D, L$ are already connected. So a decrease requires $U, L, i$ of one colour and $D$ of the other: probability $\frac18$. Expected change $\ge \frac14 - \frac18 = \frac18$.

Summing, $\mathbb E[X_{mn}] \ge 1 + \frac18(mn-1) > \frac{mn}{8}$. ∎

(Adding a whole row at a time does not work so simply: one new row can merge many regions at once.)

putnam-2004-a6.title: A four-variable square
putnam-2004-a6.body:
Let $F(x,y,z,w) = f(x,y) + f(z,w) - f(x,w) - f(z,y)$, continuous on $[0,1]^4$, so $\int_{[0,1]^4}F^2 \ge 0$. Use the notation
$$Q = \iint f^2,\quad S = \iint f,\quad R = \int_0^1\Big(\int_0^1 f(x,t)\,dt\Big)^2dx,\quad C = \int_0^1\Big(\int_0^1 f(t,y)\,dt\Big)^2dy .$$
The inequality to prove is $C + R \le S^2 + Q$.

Expand $F^2$ and integrate each term over $[0,1]^4$ (Fubini; all functions are continuous):
- the four squares $f(x,y)^2, f(z,w)^2, f(x,w)^2, f(z,y)^2$ each give $Q$;
- $2f(x,y)f(z,w)$ and $2f(x,w)f(z,y)$ involve disjoint variables, each giving $2S^2$;
- $-2f(x,y)f(x,w)$ and $-2f(z,w)f(z,y)$ share only the first variable; e.g. $\int_x\left(\int_y f(x,y)\right)\left(\int_w f(x,w)\right) = R$, so they give $-2R$ each;
- $-2f(x,y)f(z,y)$ and $-2f(z,w)f(x,w)$ share only the second variable and give $-2C$ each.

Therefore
$$0 \le \int_{[0,1]^4}F^2 = 4Q + 4S^2 - 4R - 4C,$$
i.e. $R + C \le S^2 + Q$, which is the claim. ∎

(Discretized, this is the identity $\frac14\sum_{i,j,k,l}(x_{ij}+x_{kl}-x_{il}-x_{kj})^2 = \text{RHS} - \text{LHS}$ for an $n\times n$ array.)

putnam-2004-a6.title: Orthogonal decomposition
putnam-2004-a6.body:
Let $\alpha(x) = \int_0^1 f(x,y)\,dy$, $\beta(y) = \int_0^1 f(x,y)\,dx$, $S = \iint f$, and write
$$f(x,y) = S + a(x) + b(y) + r(x,y),\qquad a = \alpha - S,\ b = \beta - S,\ r = f - \alpha(x) - \beta(y) + S .$$
Then $\int_0^1 a = \int_0^1 b = 0$, and for every fixed $x$, $\int_0^1 r(x,y)\,dy = \alpha(x) - \alpha(x) - S + S = 0$; similarly $\int_0^1 r(x,y)\,dx = 0$ for every $y$. It follows that the four functions $S$, $a(x)$, $b(y)$, $r(x,y)$ are pairwise orthogonal in $L^2([0,1]^2)$: e.g. $\iint a(x)b(y) = (\int a)(\int b) = 0$ and $\iint a(x)r(x,y) = \int a(x)\left(\int r(x,y)\,dy\right)dx = 0$. Hence
$$\iint f^2 = S^2 + \int a^2 + \int b^2 + \iint r^2,\qquad \int\alpha^2 = S^2 + \int a^2,\qquad \int\beta^2 = S^2 + \int b^2 .$$
The left side of the inequality is $\int\beta^2 + \int\alpha^2$ and the right side is $S^2 + \iint f^2$, so
$$\text{RHS} - \text{LHS} = \iint r^2 \ \ge\ 0 . \qquad ∎$$

putnam-2004-b1.title: Two expressions with coprime denominators
putnam-2004-b1.body:
If $r = 0$ all the numbers are $0$. Otherwise write $r = p/q$ with $\gcd(p,q) = 1$, $q\ge1$, $p \ne 0$. For $1\le k\le n$ let
$$s_k = c_nr^k + c_{n-1}r^{k-1} + \cdots + c_{n-k+1}r = \sum_{j=1}^{k} c_{n-k+j}\,\frac{p^j}{q^j}.$$
**First,** $q^ks_k = \sum_j c_{n-k+j}p^jq^{k-j}$ is an integer.

**Second,** multiplying $s_k$ by $r^{n-k}$ gives the top part of $P(r)$:
$$r^{n-k}s_k = c_nr^n + \cdots + c_{n-k+1}r^{n-k+1} = -\left(c_{n-k}r^{n-k} + \cdots + c_1r + c_0\right),$$
since $P(r) = 0$. Dividing by $r^{n-k}$:
$$s_k = -\left(c_{n-k} + c_{n-k-1}\frac qp + \cdots + c_0\frac{q^{n-k}}{p^{n-k}}\right),$$
so $p^{n-k}s_k$ is an integer.

Since $\gcd(p^{n-k}, q^k) = 1$, there are integers $u, v$ with $up^{n-k} + vq^k = 1$, and then $s_k = u\,(p^{n-k}s_k) + v\,(q^ks_k)$ is an integer. ∎

*Remark.* Synthetic division of $P(x)$ by $x - r$ produces the numbers $s_k/r$ as the coefficients of the quotient, so $P(x) = (qx-p)\,T(x)$ where $T$ has coefficients $s_k/p$. Gauss's lemma says $T$ has integer coefficients, which is even stronger than the claim.

putnam-2004-b2.title: One term of the binomial expansion
putnam-2004-b2.body:
By the binomial theorem,
$$(m+n)^{m+n} = \sum_{k=0}^{m+n}\binom{m+n}{k}m^kn^{m+n-k}.$$
All terms are positive, and there are at least two of them, so the sum is strictly larger than its term with $k = m$:
$$(m+n)^{m+n} > \binom{m+n}{m}m^mn^n = \frac{(m+n)!}{m!\,n!}\,m^mn^n .$$
Dividing both sides by $(m+n)^{m+n}\,\frac{m^mn^n}{m!\,n!} > 0$ gives
$$\frac{m!\,n!}{m^mn^n} > \frac{(m+n)!}{(m+n)^{m+n}}. \qquad ∎$$

*Interpretation.* Draw $m+n$ times with replacement from $m$ red and $n$ blue balls. The probability of drawing every ball exactly once is $\frac{(m+n)!}{(m+n)^{m+n}}$; it equals $\Pr(\text{exactly } m \text{ red draws})\cdot\frac{m!}{m^m}\cdot\frac{n!}{n^n}$, and the first factor is $<1$.

putnam-2004-b2.title: Compare sorted factors
putnam-2004-b2.body:
Write $\frac{k!}{k^k} = \prod_{i=1}^k\frac ik$. The inequality becomes
$$\prod_{i=1}^{m}\frac im\ \prod_{j=1}^n\frac jn \ >\ \prod_{k=1}^{m+n}\frac{k}{m+n},$$
two products of $m+n$ numbers in $(0,1]$. Sort the factors on the left increasingly as $L_1\le L_2\le\cdots\le L_{m+n}$; the $k$-th smallest on the right is $\frac{k}{m+n}$.

**Claim:** $L_k \ge \frac{k}{m+n}$ for every $k$. The number of $i\in\{1,\dots,m\}$ with $\frac im < \frac{k}{m+n}$ is the number of positive integers below $\frac{km}{m+n}$, which is $< \frac{km}{m+n}$; similarly fewer than $\frac{kn}{m+n}$ of the $\frac jn$ are below $\frac{k}{m+n}$. So fewer than $k$ (hence at most $k-1$) left factors are $< \frac{k}{m+n}$, which means $L_k \ge \frac{k}{m+n}$.

Multiplying these $m+n$ inequalities between positive numbers gives "$\ge$", and the first one is strict: $L_1 = \min(\frac1m,\frac1n) > \frac1{m+n}$. ∎

putnam-2004-b3.title: Rectangle, and a perimeter bound
putnam-2004-b3.body:
**Answer: all $a > 2$.**

**$a > 2$ works.** Take the constant $f(x) = h$. Then $R$ is an $a\times h$ rectangle with perimeter $2a + 2h$ and area $ah$; these are equal when $h(a-2) = 2a$, i.e. $h = \frac{2a}{a-2} > 0$. Then $k = \frac{2a^2}{a-2}$.

**$a \le 2$ fails.** Let $f\ge0$ be continuous on $[0,a]$ and let $P = (x_0, y_0)$ be a point of the graph where $f$ attains its maximum $y_0$ (it exists by compactness).
- *Area:* $R$ lies in the rectangle $[0,a]\times[0,y_0]$, so $\mathrm{area}(R) \le ay_0$.
- *Perimeter:* the boundary of $R$ consists of the bottom segment from $(0,0)$ to $(a,0)$ (length $a$), the left vertical segment from $(0,0)$ to $(0,f(0))$, the graph of $f$, and the right vertical segment from $(a,f(a))$ to $(a,0)$. The points $(0,0)$, $P$, $(a,0)$ cut the boundary into three arcs. The arc from $(0,0)$ to $P$ (up the left side and along the graph) has length at least the distance from $(0,0)$ to $P$, which is $\ge y_0$; likewise the arc from $P$ to $(a,0)$. (If the graph is not rectifiable, the perimeter is infinite and cannot equal a finite area.) So $\mathrm{perimeter}(R) \ge a + 2y_0$.

Since $a\le2$: $ay_0 \le 2y_0 < 2y_0 + a$. Thus perimeter $>$ area for every such $f$, and no $k$ exists. ∎

putnam-2004-b4.title: Complex numbers
putnam-2004-b4.body:
Identify the plane with $\mathbb C$, so $P_k = k$, and let $\zeta = e^{2\pi i/n}$. The rotation about $k$ is
$$R_k(z) = k + \zeta(z-k) = \zeta z + k(1-\zeta).$$
**Claim:** after applying $R_1,\dots,R_j$, the point $z$ goes to $\zeta^jz + (1-\zeta)\sum_{k=1}^{j}k\,\zeta^{j-k}$. For $j=1$ this is $R_1$. If it holds for $j$, applying $R_{j+1}$ gives
$$\zeta^{j+1}z + (1-\zeta)\sum_{k=1}^jk\,\zeta^{j+1-k} + (j+1)(1-\zeta) = \zeta^{j+1}z + (1-\zeta)\sum_{k=1}^{j+1}k\,\zeta^{j+1-k}.$$
For $j = n$, $\zeta^n = 1$, and with $T = \sum_{k=1}^n k\,\zeta^{n-k} = n + (n-1)\zeta + \cdots + 1\cdot\zeta^{n-1}$,
$$(1-\zeta)T = n + (n-1)\zeta + \cdots + \zeta^{n-1} - \left(n\zeta + (n-1)\zeta^2 + \cdots + \zeta^n\right) = n - (\zeta + \zeta^2 + \cdots + \zeta^n) = n,$$
because the $n$-th roots of unity $\zeta,\zeta^2,\dots,\zeta^n$ sum to $0$ ($\zeta\ne1$ as $n\ge2$). Hence $R(z) = z + n$.

**Answer:** $R(x,y) = (x+n,\ y)$, a translation by $n$ to the right.

putnam-2004-b4.title: Rolling a regular polygon
putnam-2004-b4.body:
Each $R_k$ is a rotation by $\theta$, so $R$ is an orientation-preserving isometry with total rotation angle $n\theta = 2\pi$, i.e. a **translation**; it suffices to find the image of one point.

Let $K$ be the regular $n$-gon with side $1$ lying **below** the $x$-axis with one side from $V_0 = (0,0)$ to $V_1 = (1,0)$; label its vertices $V_0, V_1, \dots, V_{n-1}$ clockwise. Its exterior angle is $\theta$, so rotating $K$ counterclockwise by $\theta$ about $V_1 = P_1$ swings $V_2$ up to $(2,0)$: the polygon "rolls" one step to the right, now resting with side $[1,2]$ on the axis. Inductively, after $R_1,\dots,R_k$ the image of $K$ lies below the axis with the images of $V_k, V_{k+1}$ at $(k,0), (k+1,0)$ (indices mod $n$), and $R_{k+1}$ rotates about $(k+1,0)$, rolling it once more. After $n$ steps the image of $V_n = V_0$ is at $(n,0)$.

So $R(0,0) = (n,0)$ and the translation is by $(n,0)$: $R(x,y) = (x+n, y)$.

putnam-2004-b5.title: Summation by parts and a Riemann sum
putnam-2004-b5.body:
Fix $0<x<1$ and take logarithms: the product is $e^{L(x)}$ with
$$L(x) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty x^n\left[\ln(1+x^{n+1}) - \ln(1+x^n)\right],$$
provided the series converges. Its partial sums rearrange as
$$\sum_{n=0}^{N}x^n\ln(1+x^{n+1}) - \sum_{n=0}^Nx^n\ln(1+x^n) = \frac1x\sum_{n=1}^{N+1}x^n\ln(1+x^n) - \sum_{n=0}^{N}x^n\ln(1+x^n)$$
$$= x^N\ln(1+x^{N+1}) - \ln 2 + \left(\frac1x - 1\right)\sum_{n=1}^{N}x^n\ln(1+x^n).$$
As $N\to\infty$, $x^N\ln(1+x^{N+1})\to0$ and the last series converges ($0\le x^n\ln(1+x^n)\le x^{2n}$). So
$$L(x) = -\ln2 + \frac{1-x}{x}\sum_{n=1}^\infty x^n\ln(1+x^n).$$

**The limit of the sum.** Put $h = -\ln x > 0$ (so $h\to0^+$ as $x\to1^-$) and $g(s) = e^{-s}\ln(1+e^{-s})$, a positive decreasing function on $[0,\infty)$ with $g(s)\le e^{-2s}$. Then $\sum_{n\ge1}x^n\ln(1+x^n) = \sum_{n\ge1}g(nh)$, and since $g$ is decreasing,
$$\int_h^\infty g(s)\,ds \ \le\ h\sum_{n=1}^\infty g(nh) \ \le\ \int_0^\infty g(s)\,ds .$$
Both bounds tend to $\int_0^\infty g$ as $h\to0^+$. With $t = e^{-s}$,
$$\int_0^\infty g(s)\,ds = \int_0^1\ln(1+t)\,dt = \Big[(1+t)\ln(1+t) - t\Big]_0^1 = 2\ln2 - 1.$$
Also $\frac{1-x}{x\,h} = \frac{1-x}{-x\ln x}\to1$. Hence
$$\lim_{x\to1^-}L(x) = -\ln2 + (2\ln2 - 1) = \ln2 - 1,$$
and by continuity of $\exp$ the requested limit is $e^{\ln2-1} = \dfrac2e$.

**Answer:** $\dfrac{2}{e}\approx 0.7358$.

putnam-2004-b5.title: Expand the logarithm as a series
putnam-2004-b5.body:
As in the first solution, $L(x) = -\ln2 + \frac{1-x}{x}\sum_{n\ge1}x^n\ln(1+x^n)$. Expand $\ln(1+x^n) = \sum_{m\ge1}\frac{(-1)^{m+1}}{m}x^{mn}$. The double series converges absolutely, since $\sum_{n}\sum_m\frac{x^{n+mn}}{m} = \sum_n x^n\left(-\ln(1-x^n)\right) \le -\ln(1-x)\sum_nx^n < \infty$, so we may sum over $n$ first:
$$\frac{1-x}{x}\sum_{n\ge1}x^n\ln(1+x^n) = \frac{1-x}{x}\sum_{m\ge1}\frac{(-1)^{m+1}}{m}\cdot\frac{x^{m+1}}{1-x^{m+1}} = \sum_{m\ge1}\frac{(-1)^{m+1}}{m}\cdot\frac{x^m}{1+x+\cdots+x^m}.$$
Since $x^m\le x^j$ for $j\le m$, the fraction $\frac{x^m}{1+x+\cdots+x^m}$ lies in $[0,\frac{1}{m+1}]$, so the $m$-th term is bounded by $\frac{1}{m(m+1)}$ uniformly in $x\in(0,1)$. By the Weierstrass M-test we may let $x\to1^-$ term by term; each fraction tends to $\frac{1}{m+1}$:
$$\lim_{x\to1^-}\sum_{m\ge1}\frac{(-1)^{m+1}}{m(m+1)} = \sum_{m\ge1}(-1)^{m+1}\left(\frac1m - \frac1{m+1}\right) = \ln2 + (\ln2 - 1) = 2\ln2 - 1,$$
using $\sum_{m\ge1}\frac{(-1)^{m+1}}{m} = \ln 2$ and $\sum_{m\ge1}\frac{(-1)^{m}}{m+1} = \ln2 - 1$. So $L\to\ln2 - 1$ and the limit is $\dfrac2e$.

putnam-2004-b6.title: Many disjoint translates
putnam-2004-b6.body:
**Disjoint translates.** Suppose $c_1 < c_2 < \cdots < c_k$ are nonnegative integers such that no difference $c_j - c_i$ ($i<j$) belongs to $\mathcal B$. Then the sets $\mathcal A + c_i = \{a + c_i : a\in\mathcal A\}$ are pairwise disjoint: if $a + c_i = a' + c_j$ with $i<j$, then $a - a' = c_j - c_i > 0$ is in $\mathcal B$, a contradiction. All these sets consist of positive integers, so counting their elements up to $x$:
$$\sum_{i=1}^k N(x - c_i) \le x .$$
Since $N(x - c_i) \ge N(x) - c_i$ (at most $c_i$ integers lie in $(x-c_i, x]$), we get $kN(x) \le x + \sum_i c_i$, hence
$$\limsup_{x\to\infty}\frac{N(x)}{x} \le \frac1k .$$

**Construction.** The hypothesis implies $\mathcal B$ is infinite and contains arbitrarily long runs of consecutive positive integers not in $\mathcal B$ (between $b_i$ and $b_{i+1}$ there are $b_{i+1}-b_i-1$ of them). Start with $c_1 = 0$. Given $c_1<\cdots<c_k$ as above, choose a run of at least $c_k + 1$ consecutive positive integers outside $\mathcal B$ lying between some $b_i \ge 1$ and $b_{i+1}$, and let $c_{k+1}$ be the largest element of the run. Then the run contains all of $c_{k+1} - c_k, \dots, c_{k+1} - 0$, so for each $j\le k$ the difference $c_{k+1} - c_j \in [c_{k+1}-c_k,\ c_{k+1}]$ is not in $\mathcal B$; and $c_{k+1} - c_k$ is a positive integer, so $c_{k+1}>c_k$.

Thus for every $k$ we have $\limsup N(x)/x \le 1/k$, so $\limsup N(x)/x = 0$; as $N(x)/x\ge0$, $\lim_{x\to\infty}N(x)/x = 0$. ∎

putnam-2004-b6.title: Doubling argument (extremal)
putnam-2004-b6.body:
Call $\mathcal A$ *admissible* if it satisfies the hypothesis, and let $L$ be the supremum of $\limsup N_{\mathcal A}(x)/x$ over admissible $\mathcal A$ (a number in $[0,1]$). Suppose $L>0$ and pick an admissible $\mathcal A$ with $\limsup N(x)/x > \frac34L$.

Since $\mathcal B$ has gaps, there is a positive integer $m\notin\mathcal B$; then $\mathcal A$ and $\mathcal A + m$ are disjoint (as in the first solution). Let $\mathcal A' = \mathcal A\cup(\mathcal A+m)$. Its counting function is $N(x) + N(x-m) \ge 2N(x) - m$, so $\limsup N'(x)/x \ge 2\cdot\frac34 L > L$. Hence $\mathcal A'$ is **not** admissible.

But every positive difference of elements of $\mathcal A'$ has the form $d + em$ with $e\in\{-1,0,1\}$ and $d\in\mathcal B\cup\{0\}\cup(-\mathcal B)$. Those with $d\le0$ are at most $m$ (finitely many). So $\mathcal B' \subseteq F\cup\mathcal B\cup(\mathcal B+m)\cup(\mathcal B-m)$ with $F\subseteq\{1,\dots,m\}$. Given any $K$, take a gap $b_i<b_{i+1}$ of $\mathcal B$ with $b_{i+1}-b_i > K + 2m$; the $K$ consecutive integers just above $b_i + m$ exceed $m$ and are not in $\mathcal B$, $\mathcal B\pm m$, so none lies in $\mathcal B'$. Since $\mathcal B'\supseteq\mathcal B$ is infinite, $\mathcal B'$ has gaps longer than $K$ for every $K$: $\mathcal A'$ is admissible. Contradiction.

So $L = 0$, i.e. $\lim N(x)/x = 0$ for every admissible $\mathcal A$. ∎
